a. A suitable typical value is the median. Flying Dog has median

$$\frac{6.0+7.1}{2}=6.55\%,$$

whereas Sierra Nevada has median $5.9\%$.

b. Flying Dog generally has the higher alcohol content: its median is larger, and more of its observations lie above $7\%$.

c. Flying Dog is also more variable. Its values range from $4.7\%$ to $11.5\%$, compared with $4.4\%$ to $9.6\%$ for Sierra Nevada, and its observations are more dispersed across the stems.

Chrysler/Dodge/Jeep fell from $13.6\%$ to $9.4\%$, Ford fell from $18.3\%$ to $16.7\%$, and GM fell from $26.3\%$ to $19.1\%$. Combining Honda/Acura, Mazda, Nissan/Infiniti, Subaru, and Toyota/Lexus/Scion gives a 2010 Japanese-manufacturer share of

$$10.6+2.0+7.8+2.3+15.2=37.9\%,$$

up from $28.3\%$ in 2005. Thus, the largest clear change is the loss of share by the three U.S. groups and the gain by Japanese manufacturers. The residual categories are not perfectly comparable because the 2010 chart reports more manufacturer groups separately.

a. The test statistic is

$$t=\frac{5.46-6}{2.4755/\sqrt{100}}=-2.181,$$

with $df=99$. The left-tail p-value is approximately $0.0158$. Since $0.0158<0.05$, reject $H_0$. The sample provides evidence that the population mean waiting time is less than 6 minutes.

a. The mean is $\bar{x}=36$ days and the sample standard deviation is $s\approx5.0166$ days.

b. The two-standard-deviation interval is

$$36\pm2(5.0166)=[25.967,46.033].$$

All 13 observations lie in this interval, so the observed percentage is $100\%$. For an approximately normal population, the Empirical Rule predicts about $95.44\%$; the difference is plausible for a sample of only 13 observations.

c. A 60-day time has

$$z=\frac{60-36}{5.0166}\approx4.78.$$

It is therefore extremely unusual under the approximate normal model, although not logically impossible.

The coefficient of variation is $CV=(s/\bar{x})\times100\%$. Thus,

$$CV_{\text{Fidelity}}=\frac{10.02}{17.98}\times100\%\approx55.73\%,$$

$$CV_{\text{Baron}}=\frac{12.23}{16.43}\times100\%\approx74.44\%.$$

Baron has greater variability relative to its mean return and is therefore riskier by this measure. An investor whose stated objective is lower relative risk should choose Fidelity. This comparison alone does not determine the best choice for every investor because preferences and other risk measures may differ.
